This study was conducted under a protocol approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board (approval number: 2024P003332).
Subjects were categorised into four classes: normal, early AMD, intermediate AMD, and advanced AMD (including both geographic atrophy and neovascular AMD).

Subjects were classied as having non-vision-threatening DR (no DR, mild non-proliferative DR, or moderate non-proliferative DR) or vision-threatening DR (severe non-proliferative DR or proliferative DR).

Subjects were categorised as normal (visual eld mean deviation ≥ -1 dB and otherwise relatively normal pattern standard deviation) or glaucoma (visual eld mean deviation < -3 dB with abnormal pattern standard deviation).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and glaucoma are leading causes of preventable blindness, yet whether external eye photographs carry phenotypic information about posterior segment disease remains unclear, and methods to mitigate demographic disparities in such models are largely unexplored.

We developed and evaluated deep learning and vision-language models for binary classication of vision-threatening DR (VTDR), advanced AMD, and glaucoma using 40,687 external eye photographs from 9,878 patients at Massachusetts Eye and Ear.

Convolutional networks (WResNet, EcientNet), a vision transformer (ViT), and a ne-1 NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice.

tuned vision-language model (LLaVA) were assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with fairness across sex, race, and ethnicity quantied by the equity-scaled AUC (ES-AUC).
Five fairnesstraining strategies were applied to the best models.

LLaVA achieved the highest baseline AUC for VTDR (85•4%, comparable to ViT 82•6%); advanced AMD was similar across architectures (EcientNet 86•3%; LLaVA 84•8%; ViT 84•7%), whereas glaucoma was substantially worse (6774%).
Fairness training improved VTDR and AMD AUCs to 86•3% and 85•9% while partially mitigating demographic disparities.

In summary, although AI models that rely on external eye photography to detect posterior segment disease may not yet be suitable for clinical deployment, the fairness methods demonstrated in this proof-of-concept study could be applied to other AI systems to decrease performance disparities and potentially improve model performance.

Diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and glaucoma are among the leading causes of blindness in the United States, collectively aecting over 20 million Americans. [1] Due to the high volume nature of ophthalmology and widespread use of in-clinic imaging, articial intelligence (AI) is poised to augment ophthalmic clinical care, including disease diagnosis and predicting disease progression and forecasting.

text.text: Specif-ically, there exist several high-performing models for diagnosis of posterior segment disease such as DR, glaucoma, and AMD using fundus photographs, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and more recently optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA).

More recently, there has been growing interest in whether deep learning can identify latent disease-associated information or systemic data from imaging modalities not traditionally used for standard-of-care diagnosis. [2, 3] External eye photographs represent a unique opportunity for AI-based analysis of periocular and orbital biomarkers associated with intraocular disease and systemic health status.

Image signal beyond demographic factors To assess whether model performance reected genuine image-based signal rather than demographic shortcuts (e.g., inferring age or race from periocular features), we compared each image model against a demographics-only baseline (logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees on age, race, and ethnicity), using the better-performing baseline as the comparator with 100-fold patient-clustered bootstrap 95% condence intervals and paired tests.

For DR, demographics alone achieved an AUC of 74•2%, and all image models signicantly exceeded this baseline (ViT +8•4%, 95% CI 5•511•8; EcientNet +4•4%, 0•58•1; WResNet +4•0%, 0•47•4; all 95% CIs excluding zero), indi-cating that the DR models captured substantial image-specic information beyond demographic risk.

For advanced AMD, demographics alone achieved a higher AUC of 82•6%, reecting the age dependence of AMD; the image added a smaller but signicant increment (EcientNet +3•8%, 95% CI 2•2 5•6; ViT +2•1%, 0•13•8), whereas WResNet did not signicantly exceed the baseline (+0•4%, -1•62•3).

For glaucoma, demographics alone performed near chance (AUC 55•0%) and the image models exceeded this baseline by a wide margin (ViT +18•9%, 95% CI 16•321•2; EcientNet +12•7%; WResNet +12•4%; all 95% CIs excluding zero), indicating that external photographs carry glaucoma-associated signal beyond demographics even though absolute performance remained modest (Supplementary Tables S8S9).

Discussion In proof-of-concept study, we assessed a spectrum of deep learning model architectures and fairness training methods for detecting vision-threatening DR, advanced AMD, and glaucoma from external eye photographs.

Our study has three key ndings: (1) DL models demonstrated high performance in identifying vision-threatening DR and AMD from external eye photographs; (2) VLMs such as LLaVA performed comparably to the best conventional architectures, with no statistically signicant superiority; and (3) fairness training methods improved both overall performance and subgroup performance for DR across various demographic groups, in single training runs and with the caveats on minority-group case counts discussed below.
Our rst key nding was that DL models demonstrated high performance in identifying vision-threatening DR and AMD from external eye photographs.

These ndings underscore the potential for AI-assisted biomarker exploration for posterior segment disease, and that external eye photographs may hold useful data for stratifying disease vs non-disease states.
There are several possible explanations for the predictive ability of these models.
First, DL models may detect subtle features of the fundus visible within corneal reections.

Second, external structural changes associated with systemic conditions (e.g., diabetic cornea changes, age-related periocular changes, diabetic cataracts) may increase pre-test probability for posterior segment diseases.
Saliency maps for both DR and AMD frequently highlighted the pupil and the red reex, as well as the irisscleral junction, and less frequently the adnexal features.
We therefore investigated whether the signal depends on a pharmacologically dilated pupil.

In the 857 test images with an undi-lated pupil, discriminatory power persisted for both vision-threatening DR and advanced AMD, although with lower point estimates and wide condence intervals (Supplementary Table S17).

text.text: Previous studies of external eye photographs have found that predictions of DR and systemic biomarkers generalised from undilated to dilated pupils and relied predominantly on the central region of the image (sclera, iris and pupil) rather than the eyelids. [3] These observations argue against the claim that the signal consists exclusively of a low-resolution image of the fundus through a dilated pupil.

text.text: However, we cannot rule out the possibility that the red reex contributes part of the signal.
To resolve this issue, an explicit experiment involving pupil masking and subsequent retraining is needed.

Consistent with prior work showing that external eye photographs encode systemic biomarkers,[2, 3] all DR models, and the leading AMD and glaucoma models, captured signal signicantly beyond a demographics-only baseline.
Because this baseline already conditioned on age, race, and ethnicity, the image-specic increment cannot be attributed to these demographic factors alone.
This increase was greatest for DR, for which a plausible biological mechanism has been proposed.

External eye photographs have been shown to encode information about glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c),[2, 3] and elevated HbA1c is itself an independent risk factor for vision-threatening DR (odds ratio ≈1•33 per 1% increase),[7] so the strong DR signal beyond demographic variables may arise from glycaemia-related oculomic features rather than from demographic information.
A comparable, though more tentative, rationale may apply to AMD.

Alterations in systemic lipid metabolism have been reported in AMD and linked to disease stage,[8, 10, 9, 32] and external eye photographs can encode circulating markers including blood lipids,[3] so the modest but signicant AMD signal beyond demographics may likewise reect genuine oculomic correlates.

We nonetheless present these mechanisms as plausible hypotheses rather than established explanations, and acknowledge that periocular changes correlated with age or other systemic factors may also contribute.

However, it is important to acknowledge that these saliency heat maps do not necessarily explain biological mechanisms for disease classication, but rather give external insight into important pixel-level data that informed its decision.

Therefore, a key limitation of our study is that there remains no obviously biological explanations for which external eye photographs may classify posterior segment disease besides the pixel-level information shown and the above hypotheses.

Future work on pupil masking and the red reex, certain adnexal or extraocular features, or possibly segmentation of the external vascular system may facilitate better understanding of how these models work in predicting posterior segment disease.

Ultimately, these ndings support the growing body of oculomics literature demonstrating the eye as a window to systemic health.[ 33] Of note, it is important to acknowledge that external eye photographbased models did not outperform fundus photograph-based models; as such, the goal of our study was not to demonstrate that our methodology can or should serve as a screening tool for eye disease, but rather to demonstrate the proof-of-concept utility of using external eye photographs for posterior segment disease classication.

Prior DL models for vision-threatening DR from fundus photographs achieved AUCs of 9697%,[34, 35] and glaucoma models achieved AUCs of 8291%.[ 36, 37] Although the image models significantly exceeded a demographics-only baseline for glaucoma (ViT +18•9%, 95% CI 16•321•2), absolute discrimination remained modest (AUC 6774%).

This ceiling most plausibly reects a fundamental constraint of external-eye imaging rather than a shortfall of model capacity or training data: glaucoma is dened by damage to the optic nerve head and retinal nerve bre layer (posterior structures not visible in external photographs), and its reference standard depends on functional visual-eld testing, which need not have any external ocular correlate.

This contrasts with diabetic retinopathy and advanced AMD, whose systemic and microvascular determinants (glycaemic and vascular status in DR; ageing-and lipid-related changes in AMD) may leave detectable signatures in the external eye and periocular tissues.
Glaucoma may simply lack a comparably strong, externally expressed biomarker.
Our second key nding is that the VLM performed at least as well as the strongest conventional architectures, without statistically signicant superiority.

LLaVA achieved the highest AUC for DR (85•4% vs 82•6% for ViT), whereas for advanced AMD a convolutional network (EcientNet, 86•3%) was numerically highest and LLaVA (84•8%) and ViT (84•7%) were comparable, with overlapping 95% condence intervals across the leading models.

This pattern is consistent with prior work reporting comparable performance of VLMs to transformers on healthcare tasks,[38] and high performance of ne-tuned LLaVA on chest X-ray classication.[ 39] A potential explanation may lie in the optimisation of vision-based tasks using LLaVA's vision-language connector,[26] which facilitates ecient knowledge transfer from diverse training sources.

Our models performed comparably to those published by Babenko et al (AUC 0•790•86), despite their larger training cohort.[ 3] Future work is needed to explore applications of VLMs in other imaging diagnostic applications, as well as novel use cases including image report generation and dierential disease generation, especially when used in a multimodal manner (text and imaging).

Our third key nding is that fairness training generally improved overall performance and reduced demographic disparities for DRin single training runs; these comparisons are subject to the caveats on run-to-run variability and minority-group case counts noted in the Limitations.
Using ViT as the baseline, most fairness optimisation methods demonstrated comparable or improved ES-AUC compared to baseline training, particularly for race-based equity.

These ndings were less pronounced for AMD, likely due to signicant demographic imbalance in our dataset (87•8% of patients with a positive nding for advanced AMD were White, while in the entire cohort there were only 4 Black patients and 9 Asian patients with a positive AMD nding).

The divergent behaviour of race-versus ethnicity-based metrics across DR and AMD (Supplementary Tables S1S2) likely reects diering subgroup case mixes and sample sizes: ethnicity was dominated by a large non-Hispanic majority with a small other stratum, whereas racial disparities were larger and more systematically reduced by fairness training for DR than for AMD.
These results highlight the interplay between data imbalance and algorithmic fairness and the need to account for both dataset and methodological components of model ne-tuning.

Because compilation of representative datasets can be resource-intensive, fairness training methods may oer a complementary approach to promote equitable screening and decrease AI bias against underrepresented demographic groups.
We additionally demonstrated similar improvements with FairLoRA in VLMs for DR.

To our knowledge, this is a novel nding within AI-based imaging diagnostics and future work should explore how fairness training could potentially improve VLM performance for disease diagnosis within other ophthalmic diseases and other medical specialties as well.

Although our experiments were conducted on external eye photographs which are not and should not be used for disease screening with currently existing models, application of these methods for existing AI model applications for posterior segment disease classication may improve model performance and decrease demographic bias, therefore potentially improving model generalization.
Our study has several limitations.
First, this was a retrospective study conducted at a single academic center with a predominantly White patient population, which may limit generalisability.
Furthermore, 98•7% of the images were acquired on Topcon platforms, so performance on other devices remains unestablished (Supplementary Tables S14S16).
External validation using independent datasets with more diverse populations and acquisition devices is therefore required prior to clinical deployment.
Second, disease labels were derived from ICD codes and clinical documentation, which may introduce label noise and misclassication.
The comparison groups were dened according to the target outcome within the clinical population and were not matched for concomitant ocular or systemic diseases.
Therefore, outcome-associated features that are not specic to the target disease, such as cataract or previous ocular surgery, may contribute to the learned signal.
Third, we performed binary classication, whereas ophthalmic diseases exist along a clinical spectrum that may dierentially aect demographic groups.
Fourth, subgroup analysesparticularly for AMDare limited by small sample sizes in underrepresented racial groups, necessitating cautious interpretation of subgroup-specic performance.
Our cohort was 80•1% White, with small minority strata (Black 4•1%, Asian 3•4%, Hispanic 5•6%).

Subgroup AUCs in these groups carried very wide condence intervals, so this imbalance imposes a ceiling on what algorithmic fairness methods can achieve, and apparent fairness gains must be interpreted cautiously and cannot substitute for representative data collection.
The overall cohort included only nine Asian patients and four Black patients with advanced AMD.
Therefore, the corresponding subgroup AUCs and race-based ES-AUC for AMD should be interpreted with considerable caution, and no claim is made regarding improvements in racial equity for AMD.
The observed improvements in race-based ES-AUC for VTDR should likewise be regarded as exploratory ndings that require independent replication in larger and more diverse cohorts.

Each model conguration was trained once; we did not repeat training across random seeds, so run-to-run variability is not captured by the bootstrap condence intervals, which quantify sampling variability of the test set only.

Dierences of a few AUC points between methods, such as those observed for sex and ethnicity, may lie within seed-to-seed variation, whereas the race ES-AUC changes for DR (1319 percentage points for adversarial debiasing, FSCL and FIS) are larger than is typically attributable to seed noise but still derive from small minority-group case counts.

Fifth, our study used external eye photographs captured on fundus-camera devices during routine clinical care, and did not assess performance of external photographs acquired by other modalities such as smartphones.

While the goal of our proof-of-concept study was to demonstrate feasibility of predicting posterior segment disease, we acknowledge that the performance of our models is insucient for clinical deployment and more work is needed to improve model performance and potentially evaluate on more easily acquired external eye photographs, such as smartphone photographs if the goal is to utilize external photography-based screening for ophthalmic disease.

As a real-world retrospective cohort, the racial and ethnic distribution of our dataset is inherently imbalanced and reects local patient demographics, referral patterns, and structural access to care.
Unlike curated benchmark datasets, clinical datasets cannot be articially balanced without altering disease prevalence and compromising external validity.

Accordingly, it is important to acknowledge that our objective was not to enforce demographic balance, but rather to evaluate model performance and mitigate demographic disparities under realistic clinical data distributions.

We demonstrate that state-of-the-art DL models and VLMs can identify vision-threatening DR and advanced AMD from external eye photographs, signal that signicantly exceeds a demographics-only baseline, thereby contributing to the growing eld of oculomics; the ne-tuned VLM performed comparably to, but not better than, the strongest conventional architectures.
We further show that fairness training can improve both overall and demographic-specic performance for DR.

These external eye models are a proof-of-concept and are not intended to replace standard-of-care fundus photography or to function as a screening tool in their current form; rather, they establish the feasibility of oculomic analysis of external eye photographs and provide fairness methods that are transferable to other ophthalmic and medical AI applications.

Getting closer to clinical readiness would require external and prospective validation in diverse, multi-site populations and acquisition on widely available devices such as smartphones, and patient stakeholders to advance equitable and cost-eective access to care.

The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board (approval number: 2024P003332), the institutional review board of record for the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Inrmary, the single participating centre.

Because this was a retrospective analysis of existing clinical images and electronic health record data, the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board waived the requirement for informed consent.
We followed the TRI-POD+AI reporting guidelines for studies developing AI prediction models.
There was no patient or public involvement in this study.
External eye photographs were obtained from patients who underwent clinical examination at the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Inrmary (MEEI) up until December 2024.
The photographs were initially stored with fundus images in a mixed dataset comprising approximately one million images.

All images were acquired using a variety of ophthalmic imaging platforms, including Clarus, Visucam, and Visucam NM/FA (Carl Zeiss Meditec); Maestro and Topcon color retinal imaging cameras (Topcon); Silverstone (Optos); and RetCam (Natus Medical).
The decision to obtain photographs from a specic machine was determined based on clinician preference and if imaging was felt indicated for documentation purposes or diagnostic assistance.
Ophthalmic photographers captured photographs as part of routine clinical care.

There was no specic protocol noted for image acquisition, and image resolution, formatting, and metadata varied by the machine used (median resolution 2672×3000 pixels; median eld of view 50 • ; stored in JPEG format; 95•7% of images acquired after pharmacological dilation).
Device groups were derived from the device labels contained in the image le names and represent broad imaging platforms rather than conrmed individual camera models.

Images labelled Topcon accounted for 98•7% (40,174 of 40,687) of images, with the remainder consisting of images labelled Zeiss (130), RetCam (17) or Optos (2) and unlabelled images (364) (Supplementary Table S14).
Patients of all age groups were included; age was dened as the patient's age at the time the rst image for the study was acquired.
We employed a three-step procedure to identify external eye photographs.
First, 3,000 randomly sampled images were manually reviewed and categorized into three classes: (1) external eye photographs, (2) fundus images, and (3) unusable images.
Unusable images were dened as overexposed images resulting in a completely white image, test images of the device, and images of the room without a human subject.

Second, these annotated images were used to train a previously developed deep learning classier based on the EcientNet architecture, which was subsequently applied to identify candidate external eye photographs.

Third, four trained medical re-searchers independently reviewed all candidate images and classied them as dilated external photographs, undilated external photographs, non-external photographs, unsure, or unusable.
Images classied as "unsure" by a reviewer were subsequently assessed by a senior grader for nal adjudication.

Unusable images were external eye photographs (not fundus images) that were unsuitable for analysis; reasons for unusability included fully closed eyelids, a non-visible iris, previous keratoprosthesis (KPro) surgery, the presence of corneal uorescein dye, and acquisition under a non-standard illumination lter.
This process resulted in a nal dataset of 40,687 external eye photographs from 9,878 unique patients.
Demographic variables including sex, race, ethnicity, and primary language were extracted from the electronic health record.
Self-reported sex was dened as male and female.
Race and ethnicity were self-reported by patients at registration.
Race categories included Asian, Black or African American, White, and Other (including multiple races and unknown).
Ethnicity was categorised as Hispanic, non-Hispanic, or unknown.
Disease Denitions Disease labels were obtained from clinical diagnoses and the electronic health record as follows: AMD diagnosis was based on International Classication of Diseases (ICD-10) codes.
Subjects were categorised into four classes: normal, early AMD, intermediate AMD, and advanced AMD (including both geographic atrophy and neovascular AMD).
For this study, we performed binary classication of advanced AMD versus all other categories.
ICD-10 codes have been assigned by treating ophthalmologist and DR severity followed the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy Severity Scale.
DR diagnosis was based on ICD-10 codes.

Subjects were classied as having non-vision-threatening DR (no DR, mild non-proliferative DR, or moderate non-proliferative DR) or vision-threatening DR (severe non-proliferative DR or proliferative DR).

For both DR and AMD, the comparison group therefore comprised all other patients in the cohort, including those with less severe stages of the same disease and those with other ocular diagnoses, rather than healthy controls.

Comparison groups were not matched for concomitant ocular disease, because the aim was to detect advanced disease within a real-world clinical population rather than to isolate disease-specic features under a matched case-control design.
Due to variability in clinician input ICD codes across patients, glaucoma diagnosis was dened based on visual eld metrics rather than ICD codes.

Subjects were categorised as normal (visual eld mean deviation ≥ -1 dB and otherwise relatively normal pattern standard deviation) or glaucoma (visual eld mean deviation < -3 dB with abnormal pattern standard deviation).

text.text: Fair identity scaling (FIS) is a fairness approach tailored to medical AI, which views fairness as both a group-level and identity-level problem.

It proposes an identity-level scaling mechanism that downweights patients the model already performs well on, while emphasizing patients with poorer generalization, who often belong to minority groups.
Further-ables ne-tuning with a reduced number of trainable parameters by adding trainable low-rank parameters to the pre-trained weights.
Specically, for a pre-trained weight matrix W 0 ∈ R m×n , the ne-tuned weight is written as where A ∈ R m×r and B ∈ R r×n , with small rank r.

The resulting low-rank update admits an equivalent formulation via singular value decomposition (SVD), where U ∈ R m×r and V ∈ R n×r are the left and right singular vector matrices and S ∈ R r×r is a diagonal singular value matrix; the singular vectors capture global structural directions across the embedding space, while the singular values control the relative importance of each direction.
FairLoRA extends this framework to incorporate group fairness by disentangling shared and group-specic components of the low-rank update.

For a demographic group g, FairLoRA denes the LoRA weights as where U and V are shared across all demographic groups (capturing intergroup relationships) and S g is a group-specic singular value matrix (preserving intra-group distinctiveness).
In this study, we applied FairLoRA to LLaVA-7B with LoRA rank r = 8 and scaling factor α = 16 to evaluate the impact of fairness-aware ne-tuning on VLM performance.
